lessons.title: Software Engineering at Google
lessons.authors: Titus Winters, Tom Manshreck and Hyrum Wright
lessons.summary: How to keep software changeable, understandable and economically sustainable as years, teams and dependencies accumulate.
lessons.evidenceNote: This is a practitioner account of Google's engineering practices, not a universal recipe. Its strongest value is as a set of explicit trade-offs tested at unusual scale; smaller organisations should adapt the mechanisms to their own lifespan and coordination costs.

ideas.title: Engineer for change, not just correctness today
argument: The authors distinguish programming from software engineering by adding time, scale and trade-offs. Programming asks whether code works now. Software engineering also asks whether the organisation can still change that code safely and economically throughout its useful life.

Their definition of sustainability is practical: a project is sustainable when it retains the capability to respond to valuable technical or business changes. It does not require performing every possible upgrade.
ideas.extension: Maintainability is preserved optionality. A system is healthier when future engineers can alter it without heroic knowledge, risky rewrites or frozen dependencies.
ideas.imageAlt: A timeline from code working today, through a future change, to the question of whether the software remains adaptable years later.
ideas.imageCaption: Software engineering stretches the programming decision across the system's expected life.
ideas.why: A shortcut can be rational for a three-week prototype and reckless for a ten-year business system. Expected lifespan should influence investment in tests, interfaces, automation, documentation, migration paths and consistency.
apply: Pick one component you expect to survive for several more years. Name one plausible change that would be disproportionately difficult: a vendor replacement, identity change, data migration, new client or new regulatory rule.
Write the smallest move that would preserve the option to make that change later. Do not build the future feature; reduce one source of avoidable lock-in.
ideas.caveat: Future-proofing can become speculative over-engineering. Preserve capability for plausible changes with asymmetric consequences, not every imaginable future.
questions: In your own words, what do time, scale and trade-offs add to the idea of programming?
A small internal application may run for eight years but depends directly on a vendor API throughout the codebase. What would you change now, and what would you deliberately leave alone?

ideas.title: Observable behaviour becomes part of your API
argument: Hyrum's Law states that, with enough users of an API, every observable behaviour will eventually be depended on by somebody, whether or not it was documented as part of the contract. Ordering, error text, timing, default values, whitespace, side effects and quirks can all become dependencies.
The practical lesson is not that APIs can never change. It is that the real compatibility surface is usually larger than the promised one.
ideas.extension: Treat compatibility as an observation problem before treating it as a documentation argument. Telemetry, consumer tests and staged migrations reveal dependencies that the written contract cannot.
ideas.imageAlt: Consumers depending on undocumented API behaviours such as defaults, ordering, timing, side effects and error text.
ideas.imageCaption: If a consumer can observe a detail, somebody may eventually rely on it.
ideas.why: Apparently harmless refactors can break production consumers because compatibility risk grows from what users can observe, not merely what the specification promises.
apply: Choose one API, database view, file export or shared component. List three observable behaviours that are not explicitly guaranteed.
Classify each as safe to change, change only with telemetry or migration, or effectively part of the contract now.
ideas.caveat: Hyrum's Law is an engineering observation, not a mathematical law. A small system with known consumers can often change behaviour safely after checking them directly.
questions: Why can an undocumented behaviour still function as part of an API contract?
You want to change the ordering returned by an internal endpoint because no order was promised. What evidence should you gather before shipping?

ideas.title: Code review is a knowledge-distribution system
argument: The book treats code review as more than defect detection. A well-designed process also improves comprehension, consistency, shared ownership, knowledge transfer and the historical record of why a change was made.

Google's account explicitly acknowledges the cost: review adds latency and can become unsustainable when it is heavyweight. Small changes, prompt feedback and automation keep the human attention focused on judgement.
ideas.extension: Review reduces key-person risk only when it transfers context. The asset being distributed is not approval; it is enough understanding for someone else to maintain and challenge the change.
ideas.imageAlt: A small code change moving from author to reviewer, spreading knowledge to other maintainers and preserving rationale in review history.
ideas.imageCaption: A good review turns one person's context into shared ownership.
ideas.why: When only one developer understands an area, every future change queues behind that person. Review can gradually spread comprehension and make ownership less fragile.
apply: For the next meaningful review, ask: What assumption does this change rely on that the next maintainer is least likely to know?
If it matters, move that rationale into the code, test, change description or durable documentation. A review-only explanation may disappear from where future readers need it.
ideas.caveat: Mandatory review can become ceremony or a gatekeeper queue. Optimise for small changes, fast first responses, clear reviewer roles and automated checks; do not confuse more reviewers with better review.
questions: Besides catching defects, which two long-term benefits of code review matter most, and why?
A senior developer reviews nearly every change because they know the system best, but delivery queues behind them. How would you spread knowledge without simply removing review?

experiment.title: Run a changeability scan
steps: Choose one long-lived component you actively own.
Write one plausible change it may face in the next two years.
Identify the single assumption or dependency that would make that change hardest.
Write one follow-up action that would take less than a day to implement later.
experiment.result: Finish this sentence: If X changes, Y is our biggest obstacle, so the next cheap move is Z.

spacedRecall: From The Goal: how would you distinguish the current system constraint from a stage that merely looks busy?
From The Design of Everyday Things: what might a code review interface be teaching when authors send enormous changes for review?
lessons.takeaway: Good software engineering preserves the organisation's ability to change its mind later without paying a heroic price.

sources.label: Official online edition: What Is Software Engineering?

lessons.title: Thinking in Systems
lessons.summary: A compact language for seeing the structures beneath recurring events—and finding interventions with more leverage than another local fix.
lessons.evidenceNote: Meadows presents a rigorous conceptual toolkit rather than a predictive formula. System maps are useful hypotheses about causality; they should be tested against observations and revised when people, incentives or outside conditions contradict them.

ideas.title: Events are the surface, not the system
argument: Meadows defines a system through elements, interconnections and a function or purpose. Its behaviour over time emerges from stocks, flows, feedback loops and delays—not just from the latest visible event.
When a pattern repeats, explaining the most recent incident may be true but incomplete. The stronger question is what structure keeps making this class of incident likely.
ideas.extension: In product and engineering work, recurring release pain is often maintained by a loop: pressure encourages larger batches, large batches make review and testing harder, failures create more governance, and governance increases the pressure to batch.
ideas.imageAlt: A feedback loop showing work entering a queue, a bottleneck creating rework, and rework returning to the queue.
ideas.imageCaption: Recurring results often come from a loop, not one bad event.
ideas.why: Incident fixes matter, but a recurring pattern normally changes only when the structure producing it changes. Seeing the loop prevents repeated blame from masquerading as analysis.
apply: Choose one recurring delivery problem and draw four nodes: trigger, action, short-term benefit and delayed consequence.
Add the arrow that makes the original trigger more likely next time. That arrow is often where the system stops looking like a sequence and starts looking like a loop.
ideas.caveat: A tidy diagram can omit power, incentives, emotions and external constraints. Treat the map as a testable model, not as the system itself.
questions: Why is a recurring pattern stronger evidence of system structure than a single event?
A release fails, so management adds another approval; releases then become larger and riskier. What reinforcing loop might be operating?

ideas.title: Delays create surprises
argument: Meadows shows that feedback often arrives after a delay. A decision can be sensible and the system can be responding correctly while the result remains invisible for days, months or years.

When decision-makers react faster than the system can reveal consequences, they overshoot, reverse too late and create oscillation. Delays are therefore part of the causal structure, not administrative detail.
ideas.extension: Make two clocks explicit in product decisions: when a leading signal can appear and when the outcome that matters can be judged. This reduces the temptation to declare victory—or failure—from an early proxy.
ideas.imageAlt: A timeline showing an action, an invisible delay, an early signal and a later outcome.
ideas.imageCaption: Make the time between action and consequence visible before reacting again.
ideas.why: Teams often over-correct because the last intervention has not had time to work. Naming the delay improves pacing and helps separate an early signal from the real outcome.
apply: For one current product or process change, write the earliest date you expect a leading signal and the earliest date the customer or business outcome can be judged.
Decide in advance what evidence would justify intervening before the second date.
ideas.caveat: Waiting can become an excuse for inaction. When harm is large or irreversible, use guardrails and leading indicators rather than waiting passively for lagging outcomes.
questions: How can a delay make a correctly responding system appear unresponsive?
A team changes onboarding and daily activation drops for two days while 30-day retention is the goal. What should it monitor before reversing the change?

ideas.title: Change the rules before pushing the people
argument: Meadows' leverage-points framework ranks places to intervene. Parameters such as numbers and budgets can matter, but information flows, rules, goals and paradigms can reshape many downstream decisions at once.
The ranking is a heuristic, not a promise that deeper intervention is easy. Systems often resist changes near high-leverage points precisely because those places organise power and behaviour.
ideas.extension: Before asking people to be more careful, inspect what the workflow makes visible and rewarding. A system that displays speed immediately but hides rework for weeks will predictably privilege speed.
ideas.imageAlt: A stack of intervention layers rising from numbers and targets through rules and information to goals and mindset.
ideas.imageCaption: Deeper interventions can reshape many downstream choices—but carry broader consequences.
ideas.why: A rule, information channel or goal can change hundreds of local choices without supervising each one. That is leverage: changing the conditions under which decisions make sense.
apply: Choose one behaviour you keep requesting from a team. Write what the current metric, approval rule or information flow rewards instead.
Propose one reversible change to that condition and name the side effect you will watch.
ideas.caveat: High leverage also means high blast radius. Change rules and goals with the people living in the system, test reversibly where possible and monitor unintended adaptation.
questions: Why might changing an information flow have more leverage than increasing a target?
A service desk is rewarded for tickets closed, while repeat contacts are invisible. What rule or information change would you test first?

experiment.title: Draw one loop, not one blame story
steps: Choose a frustrating result that has happened at least three times.
Draw four boxes: trigger, action, short-term benefit and later consequence.
Add the arrow showing how the consequence makes the trigger more likely.
Mark one delay and one piece of missing information in the loop.
experiment.result: You finish with one causal-loop hypothesis and one observation that could prove it wrong.

lessons.takeaway: When the same problem returns, stop pushing harder on the event and look for the loop, delay or rule that keeps recreating it.

sources.label: Donella Meadows Project: Dancing With Systems

lessons.title: The Design of Everyday Things
lessons.summary: When users repeatedly make the same mistake, the interface may be teaching the wrong action.
lessons.evidenceNote: Norman's framework combines established ideas from cognitive psychology with practical design principles. It is strongest as a diagnostic language for discoverability, mental models and error resilience—not as proof that one interface pattern works for every user or culture.

ideas.title: Make the right action visible
argument: Norman distinguishes affordances—relationships that make actions possible—from signifiers: perceptible clues showing where and how to act. Signifiers became more prominent in the revised edition because digital interfaces can support many invisible actions.
A control can technically afford an action while remaining functionally undiscoverable. Repeated requests for help with an ordinary task may be evidence of weak signalling rather than weak users.
ideas.extension: In software, wording, position, grouping, state and feedback all signify. A familiar icon can still fail when its placement or visual priority tells the wrong story.
ideas.imageAlt: Two doors with the same physical affordance: one ambiguous and one clearly labelled push.
ideas.imageCaption: The possible action may be identical; the visible cue changes whether it is discovered.
ideas.why: A user should not need to reverse-engineer the designer's intention. Clear signifiers reduce hesitation, support learning and prevent repeated support questions.
apply: Pick one screen and identify its most important next action. Imagine a first-time user with no documentation: what visible cue tells them what to do?
If the answer is mostly 'they should know', strengthen one cue and define an observable measure such as completion rate, hesitation time or support contacts.
ideas.caveat: More signalling is not automatically better. Labels, icons, badges and hints can compete until none has priority. Aim for enough information for the intended action to be inferred correctly.
questions: What is the difference between an affordance and a signifier, and why does it matter in software?
A small grey icon opens an important approval workflow, but users keep asking support how to approve requests. What would you change first, and what evidence would show improvement?

ideas.title: Give users a correct conceptual model
argument: People build simplified explanations of how systems work. Good design helps them form a useful conceptual model so they can predict what actions will do and interpret system state.

Norman's thermostat example shows the cost of a wrong model: with a simple on/off thermostat, setting a much higher target does not make heating faster; it only changes when heating stops. A user can act rationally from the model the interface appears to teach and still be wrong.
ideas.extension: Product teams often explain screens instead of repairing the system image. If users misunderstand the workflow's rules, another tooltip may treat the symptom while preserving the wrong model.
ideas.imageAlt: A thermostat contrasted with a guessed model that a higher target heats faster and the actual on-off model.
ideas.imageCaption: A coherent model lets users predict behaviour beyond memorised instructions.
ideas.why: Once users understand how a system behaves, they can reason through unfamiliar cases. A wrong model produces systematic errors that training alone may not remove.
apply: Choose one confusing workflow and write two sentences: 'Users seem to believe…' and 'The system actually…'.
If they differ, find the status name, sequence, wording or feedback teaching the wrong model.
ideas.caveat: Conceptual models are simplifications. Exposing internal architecture can make the product harder to understand; the model only needs enough fidelity to predict relevant behaviour.
questions: Why can a technically correct interface still cause systematic mistakes?
Users think Submit immediately sends data externally, but it actually enters an internal validation queue. How would you redesign the system image?

ideas.title: Design for error, not perfect behaviour
argument: Norman rejects the habit of treating every error as careless behaviour. A slip is the wrong action while pursuing the right goal; a mistake begins with the wrong goal, rule or plan. The two need different defences.

Constraints, interlocks, undo, confirmation, sensibility checks, safe defaults and resilience are different tools. The important design question is not only how to prevent the wrong action, but how much damage occurs after it.
ideas.extension: For consequential workflows, recoverability is a product capability. A reversible state can be more valuable than another warning because it still works when attention fails.
ideas.imageAlt: A fragile delete action leading to gone, compared with a resilient delete action leading to a recoverable trash state and undo.
ideas.imageCaption: Predictable slips become minor corrections when the system preserves recovery.
ideas.why: Undo, previews, reversible states and constraints can turn a serious incident into a small correction—even when a competent user acts under pressure.
apply: Find one destructive, financial or hard-to-reverse action. Classify its current defence as prevented, detectable, recoverable or irreversible.
If it is mostly irreversible, identify the smallest change that makes the state recoverable.
ideas.caveat: Confirmation dialogs are not a universal solution. If routine actions always ask 'Are you sure?', users learn to click through. Reserve strong friction for unusual or consequential actions.
questions: Why is designing for recovery often more effective than telling users to be careful?
An authorised administrator can permanently delete a customer with one click. Which constraints and recovery mechanisms would you combine, and which would you avoid overusing?

experiment.title: Run a usability archaeology test
steps: Open one screen without touching anything.
Write the three actions a new user would probably think are available.
Compare them with the three actions the product actually wants them to take.
Circle the largest mismatch and classify it as a weak signifier, wrong conceptual model or poor error design.
experiment.result: You finish with one classified design problem and one observable behaviour to measure after changing it.

spacedRecall: From Team Topologies: if a capable team keeps losing time to context switching, how would you distinguish excessive cognitive load from a prioritisation problem?
lessons.takeaway: When users repeatedly do the wrong thing, inspect what the design is teaching them before teaching the users harder.

lessons.title: The Goal
lessons.authors: Eliyahu M. Goldratt and Jeff Cox
lessons.summary: Improve the whole system by finding what actually limits it, managing flow instead of busyness and judging changes by global outcomes.
lessons.evidenceNote: The Goal is a business novel and the foundation of the Theory of Constraints, not a controlled scientific study. Its systems logic is highly transferable, but manufacturing metaphors and throughput-accounting definitions need careful adaptation in software and public-service settings.

ideas.title: The constraint sets the system's ceiling
argument: In a chain of dependent work, system output is limited by the constraint: the resource or condition that most limits progress toward the goal. Improving a non-constraint may raise local output while leaving total throughput unchanged.
A constraint need not be a machine. In knowledge work it may be review capacity, a test environment, a specialist, release governance, unclear product decisions or even insufficient demand.

The wider Theory of Constraints turns this into five focusing steps: identify the constraint, exploit the capacity already available, subordinate other work to that decision, elevate the constraint if necessary, then repeat when the constraint moves—without letting old policy become the next constraint.
ideas.extension: Treat constraint identification as a falsifiable hypothesis. Ask whether a small increase in this step's effective capacity would cause more completed value to leave the whole system.
ideas.imageAlt: A delivery flow where review handles three items per day while other stages handle six to eight, creating a queue and a system ceiling of three.
ideas.imageCaption: Improving a non-constraint can raise local output without changing end-to-end throughput.
ideas.why: Teams often improve places that are visible, annoying or easy to optimise. Constraint thinking ranks improvement work by effect on the system's goal.
apply: Map one active delivery stream in five to eight steps and mark where work waits longest or where scarce capacity controls the rest.
Ask: if this step gained 20% more effective capacity tomorrow, would completed value reach users faster? If not, revise the hypothesis.
ideas.caveat: Constraints move, and the first visible backlog may only be a symptom. Policy, decision latency, skills or demand can constrain the system without forming an obvious queue.
questions: Why can improving a fast, non-constrained stage produce almost no end-to-end improvement?
Completed code waits four days for review and approval. What evidence would you gather before investing in more development capacity?

ideas.title: Balance flow, not local utilisation
argument: The Goal challenges the assumption that every resource should stay busy. In a dependent system, producing faster upstream than the constraint can consume creates inventory and queues rather than useful output.
The hiking story adds variability: dependent steps cannot rely on small fluctuations neatly cancelling. Delays compound when each step must wait for the previous one.
ideas.extension: Queueing theory reinforces the direction of the effect: high utilisation combined with variability drives waiting sharply upward. The precise curve depends on the system, so there is no universal magic utilisation target.
ideas.imageAlt: An illustrative chart where waiting time rises sharply as resource utilisation approaches full capacity, especially with higher variability.
ideas.imageCaption: The relationship is illustrative, not measured data from the book: variability needs slack.
ideas.why: A reviewer booked at 100% has no capacity for urgent defects, clarification, rework or variation in task size. Everyone can look busy while delivery slows.
apply: Choose one scarce person or function and compare incoming work with available capacity over the last few weeks.
Protect flow by removing low-value demand, preparing work better, reducing rework, batching less or reserving explicit slack.
ideas.caveat: Software delivery is not a simple single-server queue, and collaboration can change capacity dynamically. Use the principle to diagnose delay; do not claim a precise utilisation threshold the evidence cannot support.
questions: Why can maximising utilisation at every step make a dependent workflow slower?
A senior reviewer is busy nearly every minute, yet turnaround worsens. Give two interventions that improve flow without asking them to work faster.

ideas.title: Measure the whole system, not the department
argument: Goldratt reframes operational decisions around throughput, inventory or investment, and operating expense. In its original business context, throughput is money generated through sales, inventory is money tied up in things intended for sale, and operating expense is the money spent turning investment into throughput.
A local cost reduction can still harm the company if it lowers throughput or traps more work and capital in the system.
ideas.extension: For software and product work, use the measures as a decision lens: useful outcomes delivered, work trapped in queues or half-finished states, and ongoing effort or spend required to produce those outcomes.
ideas.imageAlt: Three system-level tests—raise throughput, lower inventory and lower operating expense—pointing to the question of whether a change improves the whole system.
ideas.imageCaption: A local saving can be a bad trade when it reduces throughput or traps more work.
ideas.why: Tickets closed, utilisation, lines of code and departmental cost can improve while users receive value more slowly. Global measures reconnect activity to purpose.
apply: Take one improvement proposal and test its effect on useful outcomes delivered, work tied up and ongoing effort or spend.
If it only improves a local metric and has no credible system-level benefit, challenge its priority.
ideas.caveat: Throughput accounting is a management framework, not a replacement for statutory accounting. Short-term classifications can also hide long-run capacity investments; use the lens without pretending it is a complete theory of finance.
questions: What separates a local efficiency metric from a system-level measure such as throughput?
Automation saves 20 developer-hours monthly but adds an approval that slows every release. What must be measured before calling it successful?

experiment.title: Run a constraint scan
steps: Write one workflow as five to eight steps.
Circle the step with the largest queue, longest wait or scarcest capacity.
Write: I think the current constraint is ___ because ___.
Name one exploit action that protects its existing capacity and one subordinate rule that stops upstream work overwhelming it.
experiment.result: You finish with a constraint hypothesis and one testable intervention—not a full process redesign.

lessons.takeaway: The highest-leverage improvement is the place that currently limits the whole system's ability to produce its goal—not the place where the most people look busy.

lessons.title: Team Topologies
lessons.summary: Treat team boundaries and interaction patterns as part of the software-delivery system, constrained by finite cognitive capacity.
lessons.evidenceNote: Team Topologies is a practitioner framework, not a scientifically proven recipe for high performance. Limited working memory is well supported, but applying cognitive-load theory to whole teams is an organisational extension rather than a directly established causal law. This lesson uses the 2019 first-edition vocabulary; the 2025 second edition clarifies that a platform is often a grouping of team types delivering a compelling internal product, not necessarily one isolated team.

ideas.title: Treat cognitive load as an architectural constraint
argument: The authors argue that a team should own a coherent amount of software, domain knowledge, operational responsibility, tooling and business context that its members can realistically understand.

When responsibility grows too broad, delivery slows because more effort goes into navigating complexity, switching context and reconstructing knowledge. Team boundaries should therefore reflect cognitive limits, not just reporting lines.
ideas.extension: This resembles designing software for finite memory. Declaring ownership does not increase processing capacity; each application, integration, stakeholder group and specialist technology consumes part of a finite attention budget.
ideas.imageAlt: A team's capacity filled by product, codebase, operations, stakeholders, tooling and security, with another system sitting outside the manageable boundary.
ideas.imageCaption: Responsibility can outgrow the working knowledge needed for safe change.
ideas.why: A workload problem can masquerade as a performance problem. Pressure may worsen context switching, forgotten details and fragile ownership when the real issue is excessive cognitive breadth.
apply: List everything one team must understand to make a safe production change: rules, repositories, databases, deployment, infrastructure, integrations, support, approvals and stakeholders.
Circle the item consuming substantial mental effort but contributing least to the core value stream. Consider simplification, automation, platform support or reassignment.
ideas.caveat: Cognitive load can become a vague excuse for avoiding difficult work. Some complexity is intrinsic to the domain and should remain close to the people making the relevant decisions.
questions: Why does assigning another responsibility have a cost even when it creates no immediate ticket?
A capable team owns nine applications with different deployments, databases and stakeholders. What would you investigate before asking the developers to work faster?

ideas.title: Make stream-aligned teams the centre
argument: The first-edition framework defines four fundamental team types. Stream-aligned teams own a meaningful flow of work and deliver value end to end. Enabling teams build capability, complicated-subsystem teams contain specialist complexity, and a platform capability offers internal services that reduce unnecessary complexity. Later guidance emphasises that the platform may be a grouping of several team types operating as an internal product.
The supporting types exist to improve the stream-aligned team's flow, not to recreate permanent functional silos with new labels.
ideas.extension: Ask what arrangement lets a team move from a user need to a working outcome with the fewest blocking dependencies—not which department traditionally owns a technology.
ideas.imageAlt: Enabling, platform and complicated-subsystem teams supporting a central stream-aligned team that owns a flow of value.
ideas.imageCaption: Supporting team types reduce blockers and cognitive load around value delivery.
ideas.why: Functional silos can optimise specialist utilisation while creating queues between specialists. A stream-aligned design instead makes the flow of change the primary unit of optimisation.
apply: Take one recent enhancement and map its path from request through analysis, development, infrastructure, approval, deployment and support.
Mark where work stopped for another team. Target the handoff with the most waiting relative to actual work, not simply the busiest-looking group.
ideas.caveat: End-to-end ownership does not require every specialist inside every team. Deeply specialised components can justify a complicated-subsystem team, and a good platform can avoid duplicating expertise.
questions: What makes a stream-aligned team different from a traditional frontend or database team?
A feature takes two days to develop and six waiting on infrastructure and deployment groups. What boundary or service would you examine first?

ideas.title: Give every relationship an explicit interaction mode
argument: Team Topologies names three deliberate interaction modes: collaboration for high-bandwidth discovery, X-as-a-Service for consuming a capability through a clear interface, and facilitation for temporary capability-building help.

Collaboration is intentionally expensive and should usually be time-bounded. A common path is to collaborate while uncertainty is high, then evolve toward a clearer service relationship when boundaries stabilise.
ideas.extension: Many dependencies hurt because nobody has decided what the relationship is supposed to become. Naming the current mode and its exit condition turns 'work closely together' into a design decision.
ideas.imageAlt: Three team interaction modes: time-boxed collaboration that can evolve into X-as-a-Service, plus temporary facilitation that transfers capability.
ideas.imageCaption: Interaction should have a purpose, cost and condition for changing mode.
ideas.why: Without an exit condition, teams can spend months in each other's meetings and coordinate every change. Explicit modes make the dependency inspectable and adaptable.
apply: Complete: For the next month, our relationship with Team X should be ___ because ___.
Then complete: We know the interaction can change when ___. If the last blank is impossible, the dependency may have no exit condition.
ideas.caveat: Real relationships can combine modes and change by task. Use the vocabulary to clarify intent, not to force every interaction into a permanent classification.
questions: Explain the practical difference between collaboration and X-as-a-Service without repeating their definitions.
Developers have paired with another team for six months because that team owns deployment. What mode exists now, what should it become, and what must change first?

experiment.title: Run a dependency audit
steps: Open the work item or release consuming the most coordination effort.
List every external team required before value reaches the user.
Mark each C for collaboration, S for X-as-a-Service, F for facilitation or ? for unclear.
Count the question marks and choose the highest-friction unclear relationship.
experiment.result: You finish with a number and one proposed interaction mode with an exit condition.

lessons.takeaway: A team's performance depends on how much complexity it owns, where its boundaries sit and whether its dependencies have a deliberate shape.
